passage: Exam morning, ten minutes to the bell, and Kunal's phone buzzed. Samir, who always wrote "oi legend 😄" with three stickers, had written just "hi." No emoji. Kunal's heart dropped. Did I do something? His friend's greeting had changed. But then he remembered that Samir's paper was at nine and that Samir hated messages when he was nervous. He wrote back, "Good luck today. Coffee after?" Samir replied at noon with a row of stickers: "Legend! Yes! Sorry, brain was in physics mode." Kunal grinned. One short hello didn't mean anything.

qa.q: What did Samir usually write to Kunal?
qa.a: He usually wrote "oi legend" with three stickers.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he saw just "hi"?
qa.a: He felt a moment of worry that he'd done something to upset Samir. He stopped himself and remembered the exam.

qa.q: What could Kunal do when a greeting changes?
qa.a: Consider the context first, such as the exam, and check kindly instead of concluding. One missed reply or short hello is not proof.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when he wrote just "hi"?
qa.a: He was nervous and in physics mode, not upset with Kunal. He apologised once the exam was over.

grounding: A teenager's friend changes the greeting style, but reading too much into one short hello is a pitfall.

passage: Usha used to greet Vishal with "Vishu!!" and a shower of stickers. For two weeks now, she'd only nodded in the corridor. Vishal noticed. He wondered whether their friendship was cooling. He watched her laugh with others as usual, which confused him more. On Friday he said, "You've stopped sending stickers. Did I say something?" Usha looked surprised. "Oh! No. I got a new phone and lost all my sticker packs. And I've been in a hurry." She showed him. "I'll download them again tonight. Vishu!!" He laughed with relief.

qa.q: What did Usha use to greet Vishal with?
qa.a: She used to greet him with "Vishu!!" and a shower of stickers.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when Usha only nodded?
qa.a: He was unsure and a little worried the friendship was cooling. Her laughing with others confused him.

qa.q: What worked when Vishal asked her?
qa.a: He asked directly and kindly whether he'd said something. Her honest answer removed the worry.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Vishal asked?
qa.a: She was surprised because she hadn't realised the change mattered. She quickly offered to bring the greeting back.

grounding: A teenager's friend changes the greeting style, which may signal distance or nothing, and asking clears it.

passage:
"Gargi, you used to say 'Heyyy Bini!' every morning. Now it's just 'hi.' Did I do something?"
"What? No!"
"It's been a week. I thought you were upset with me."
Gargi laughed. "Binita, I've been so tired. Board prep, tuition till eight. I barely know my own name in the morning."
"So it's not me?"
"Not you at all. I still like you. I'm just a zombie."
"Okay. I was overthinking."
"Want me to go back to 'Heyyy Bini'?"
"Only if you mean it."
Gargi grinned. "Heyyy Bini."
Binita laughed. "Better."

qa.q: What did Gargi used to say every morning?
qa.a: "Heyyy Bini!"

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the greeting changed?
qa.a: Binita felt worried and unsure, thinking the shorter "hi" meant Gargi was upset with Binita.

qa.q: What did Binita do that helped?
qa.a: Binita asked Gargi directly instead of overthinking, which revealed Gargi was just tired.

qa.q: How did Gargi see the changed greeting?
qa.a: Gargi didn't mean anything by it; Gargi was just tired from board prep.

grounding: Two teenagers discuss how a change in greeting style was misread as distance, and asking cleared it up.

passage:
Every morning for a year, Kishore sent me a sun emoji. Just 🌞. It was our thing.
Then one Monday, nothing. Tuesday, nothing. Wednesday, still nothing.
I thought he was angry with me. I went over every conversation in my head.
On Thursday I finally messaged him: "Did I upset you?"
No reply. Friday at school, I asked him to his face. He looked puzzled. "My parents took my phone for a week. My maths marks."
I laughed so hard I nearly cried. I'd spent four days worrying.
Now if he misses a morning, I don't panic.
- Dilnaz

qa.q: What emoji did Kishore send every morning?
What was Dilnaz feeling when the emoji stopped?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt anxious and worried that Kishore was angry.

qa.q: What would you advise Dilnaz about missed greetings?
qa.a: Don't read too much into one missed hello; ask directly, since there may be a simple reason.

qa.q: How did Kishore see the missing emojis?
qa.a: Kishore didn't think about it; his phone had been taken for a week.

grounding: The narrator recalls reading a friend's missed digital greeting as distance, and it was only a confiscated phone.

passage:
Teacher's note, Wednesday
I've noticed that Deepak and Samir greet each other every morning with just a nod and "Sup, bro." At first I thought it was careless, even rude. But I've seen how they grin while doing it. It's clearly their way of showing they're close.
Today, though, Samir walked past Deepak without the nod. Deepak's face fell, and he sat quietly through the first period.
At break I saw them talking. Samir had just been told off by the principal and wasn't looking at anyone.
By lunch they were nodding again.
I've reminded myself not to read too much into slang greetings or one missed hello.
- Mr D'Souza

qa.q: How do Deepak and Samir greet each other every morning?
qa.a: With just a nod and "Sup, bro."

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when Samir walked past without the nod?
qa.a: Deepak felt hurt and worried, taking the missed greeting as distance.

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza learn from watching them?
qa.a: He learned that slang greetings can show closeness and that one missed hello often has a simple reason.

qa.q: How did Samir see the missed greeting?
qa.a: Samir wasn't thinking about Deepak; he was upset after being told off by the principal.

grounding: A teacher's note shows peer slang greetings as closeness and a missed greeting misread as distance.

passage:
Thursday
Yusuf has greeted me the same way since class seven: "morning dino 🦖" on the phone, and our silly three-part handshake at the gate. Today the message said just "hi." With a full stop. A FULL STOP. At the gate he gave me a nod, like I was a teacher. Then I asked if he had the maths sheet and he didn't reply all afternoon. I spent geography building a whole story: he's found cooler friends, I said something wrong on Monday, the handshake era is over. At six I made myself write, "you ok? you went full formal on me 😅". He wrote back: "sorry Rehana, phone screen cracked, typing is pain. and my uncle was at the gate, didn't want to do dino hands in front of him lol." So. One full stop and a cracked screen. Keeping the story ideas for English class.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's message say today?
qa.a: It said just "hi." with a full stop.

qa.q: What was Rehana worried about during geography?
qa.a: Rehana felt anxious and a bit hurt, reading the full stop and the nod as distance and imagining Yusuf had found cooler friends. It may also have been plain overthinking on a quiet day.

qa.q: What would you advise Rehana next time a greeting changes?
qa.a: Check before building a story: a short, light question like the six o'clock message gets the real reason faster than an afternoon of guessing.

qa.q: What was the nod at the gate like from Yusuf's side?
qa.a: For Yusuf it was just avoiding the silly handshake in front of his uncle, not pulling away, so he probably had no idea it caused worry.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a change in a greeting and one missed reply as distance, then asking and finding it meant something else.
